questions.question_text: The prevalence of psychotic disorders in prisons compared to the general population is
questions.explanation:
A rate higher by ten times (in the UK, Ref: Brugha et al., 2005) to twenty times (elsewhere), giving a prevalence rate - 2-15% has been noted in
various studies. Fazel and Danesh conducted a meta-analysis of 62 surveys from 12 countries including 22 790 prisoners wherein 3-7% of
men had psychotic illnesses, 10% major depression, and 65% a personality disorder, including 47% with antisocial personality disorder.
Prisoners were about ten times more likely to have antisocial personality disorder than the general population. Fazel, S and Danesh, J (2002)
Serious mental disorders in 23 000 prisoners: a systematic review of 62 surveys. The Lancet 359, 545-550.

questions.question_text: Which of the following behavioural treatments in sexual deviancy is an aversion technique?
questions.explanation:
Shame aversion therapy is a contentious technique for the treatment of persons practising deviant sexual acts such as transvestism,
voyeurism, paedophilia, exhibitionism and frotteurism. It consists of having the subject who is embarrassed or self-conscious about the act
he performs perform the act on demand in front of some observers. The act is made to continue for 15 to 35 min and its style kept as close
to the in vivo situation as is possible. The patient is told simply to observe himself and be aware of being observed. (Serber, 1970: Retrieved
from

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors contributes most to the risk of prison suicides?

options.text: Absence of previous contact with mental health services
Being a member of minority ethnic group

questions.explanation:
Demographic factors associated with prison suicide include white race/ethnicity (OR = 1.9), being male (OR = 1.9), and being married (OR =
1.5). Criminological factors included occupation of a single cell (OR = 9.1), detainee/remand status (OR = 4.1), and serving a life sentence (OR
= 3.9). Clinical factors were recent suicidal ideation (OR = 15.2), history of attempted suicide (OR = 8.4), having a current psychiatric diagnosis
(OR = 5.9), receiving psychotropic medication (OR = 4.2), and having a history of alcohol use problems (OR = 3.0). Black race/ethnicity was
inversely associated with suicide (OR = 0.4). (Ref: Fazel et al. J Clin Psychiatry. 2008 Nov;69(11):1721-31).

questions.question_text: A death resulting from intentional, reckless act but because of provocation or diminished responsibility is termed as
questions.explanation:
Culpable homicide (an outcome of diminished responsibility argument): Lies in-between manslaughter and homicide. There is a lack of
speci�c or evil intent to kill but murder has taken place. This can be involuntary culpable homicide where death is unintended death but
occurs as a result of an assault or as a result of negligence. Voluntary culpable homicide refers to death resulting from the intentional,
reckless act but because of provocation or diminished responsibility. McNaughton Rules: 1843- A defect of reason (impaired, not mere
failure to exercise), due to a disease of mind (not externally caused), leading to loss of appreciation of nature and quality of an act (the
o�ence; physical nature not moral) and so the accused did not realise what he was doing was wrong (either legally or morally).

questions.question_text: Which of the following syndromes is associated with military prisoners?
questions.explanation:
In 1897, a neurologist called Sigbert Ganser noted a syndrome of approximate answers to simple questions, hallucinations, clouding of
consciousness, and somatic conversion in three prisoners. This syndrome is variously described as Ganser syndrome, balderdash syndrome,
prison psychosis and nonsense syndrome. It is rare but seen more commonly among prisoners. McGrath and McKenna reported 50 cases
amongst 8000 military prisoners (Dwyer & Reid; Lancet 2004; 364: 471 –73; )

questions.question_text:

fragmented without speci�c themes. Aggressive behaviour occurs rarely. (Ref: Oxford Handbook of psychiatry-414)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is classi�ed under sane automatism?
questions.explanation:
If an individual commits an o�ence when his body is not under the control of his mind (e.g. when asleep) he is not guilty of the o�ence.
Legally this is called automatism. Two legal types of automatism are recognised: insane and sane. The distinction is based on whether the
behaviour is likely to recur: Insane automatism-due to an intrinsic cause (e.g. sleepwalking, brain tumours, epilepsy) results in an acquittal
on the grounds of insanity. Sane automatism- due to an extrinsic cause (e.g. confusional states, concussion, re�ex actions after bee stings,
dissociative states, night terrors, and hypoglycaemia) results in a complete acquittal.
